body_markdown:
John MacKichan’s family moved to Ocala, Florida, between our sophomore and junior years in high school. I was driving a stock 1936 Chevy two-door back then, and we hit it off right away. We were both hot rod nuts.


While he was at Ocala’s junior college,[John](https://www.johnmackichan.com/about-john) built a 1928 Ford pickup with a mid-’50s Pontiac engine and standard transmission. It was channeled to the max. Around the same time, I traded the ’36 Chevy for a 1931 Deluxe Model A coupe with a would-you-believe-it six-cylinder Chevy engine and a Powerglide tranny.


We went our separate ways in 1966 but got hooked back up at our 50th high school reunion. By that time John had built numerous hot rods and a Bonneville record-breaker, the[MacKinchan-Schutz Streamliner](https://www.museumofamericanspeed.org/mackichanschulz.html) . He was working at Speedway Motors then and is now curator emeritus of the Museum of American Speed. Meanwhile, I went through a number of endeavors, including restoring old Harley and Indian motorcycles.


David Royal


When I got the 1928 roadster nine years ago, it was a finished car in show condition with fewer than 300 miles on the odometer. It featured an H&H-built flathead engine using a new old stock French military copy of a ’46-48 Ford flathead, with an electric fuel pump and a thermostatically controlled radiator fan. It had an Isky 3/4 cam; Navarro 9:1 compression heads; 268-cubic-inch stroker kit; Offenhauser three-two intake manifold with three Stromberg 97 carbs (only the middle one was working; the other two were blocked off and needed work); a ’41 Ford three-speed pickup transmission; enclosed driveshaft; and a Winters Nostalgia quick-change rear end.


The frame is a 1928 Model A, and the body is a Brooksville steel reproduction body with a ’32 Ford-type dash. The windshield is a new 1928–29 type, chopped two inches. It had a 1930–31 deluxe roadster top, 16-inch Kelsey-Hayes wire wheels up front and Wheel Vintiques 15-inch wire wheels on the back, with Mickey Thompson tires. The spare tire, gas tank, and battery were in the trunk. The engine, transmission, wheels, axle, and front brakes were all painted Ford Blue. But that color just didn’t look right on a black hot rod.


Of course, no matter how nice it is, you *always* have to[make changes](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/toad-packs-four-cylinders-of-ford-banger-fury/) to a new acquisition.


David Royal


David Royal


David Royal


David Royal


David Royal


I didn’t like the battery being by the gas tank, for instance, so I got two sealed six-volt batteries and put them under the seat. And the blue paint had to go, of course, and the only color that would look right was red.


I found three more Kelsey-Hayes wheels and replaced the funky-looking rears and the straight-spoke spare with the new ones. I also added reproduction Buick finned aluminum front brake drums. The original Buick drums were flat, and I found that out the hard way: They wouldn’t accommodate the new wheels. The new finned drums have a drop center, so everything plays nicely.


I figured three carbs were too many for the engine and replaced the Offenhauser three-two manifold with a vintage Fenton two-two manifold. Then I rebuilt one of the non-functioning 97s and put it and the already-functioning 97 on the engine.[Perfect](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/this-34-ford-pickup-was-built-in-a-year-but-it-wasnt-finished-for-several-more/) .


David Royal


I am used to more than a three-speed tranny and kept reaching for the lever to shift up after it was already in third. Fortuitously, the enclosed driveshaft soon froze up because it had been assembled without lubricating a bearing in the driveshaft. This wasn’t my first bad experience with an enclosed driveshaft, so I decided to replace it with an open driveshaft and also swap out the three-speed with a BorgWarner T-5 while I was at it. This is beyond my abilities, so I took the car to a shop in North Ogden, Utah. The conversion required adapting the rear end to the open driveshaft and replacing the rear wishbone with radius rods and an adapter to mate the T-5 to the flathead.


We are at 7000 feet of elevation here, and our winters are long and cold, so I only use the car in warmer weather. Because of that, I have no need for the top, so I removed it. The car only weighs 2100 pounds and handles better in high crosswinds without the top, anyway. My Ford hot rod runs strong and is a blast to drive. And people love it.


David Royal
